lookUpPlusOnes.name: Check the Plus-Ones
lookUpPlusOnes.description: Someone gives you their first name. Return the number of extra guests they're allowed to bring in, or `"Not on the list!"` if they're not invited.

emptyList.description: Nobody's bringing anyone in when the list is empty.

whereToStart.question: Where do I even start with this?
whereToStart.answer: Picture yourself actually doing it on the door. Someone says a name, and you read down the clipboard until you spot them. It's worth noticing that the answer you have to give them isn't written next to their name on the list you're reading.

twoLists.question: There are two lists. How do they relate to each other?
twoLists.answer: Whatever you learn about *where* someone is in one list is just as true in the other. A position is a more useful thing to hold onto than a name.

whatCountsAsAMatch.question: When does a first name actually count as a match?
whatCountsAsAMatch.answer: "Brad" should get Brad Pitt in, but not Bradley Cooper. Think about what's different about those two entries at the point where the letters you were given run out. There's more than one reasonable way to make that comparison, so pick whichever one you can explain to yourself.

noSurname.question: Cher hasn't got a surname. Does that break anything?
noSurname.answer: Have another look at what your match test assumes about a list entry. If it assumes there's always something after the first name, an entry that's *only* a first name won't get past it. And going the other way, a longer name shouldn't be able to claim a shorter entry.

notOnTheList.question: What do I do when they're not on the list?
notOnTheList.answer: Then they get the string `"Not on the list!"`, exactly as written. Two things are worth thinking about here. First, at what point can you be *certain* that someone isn't on the list? Second, notice that this is a genuinely different answer from a guest who's invited but allowed 0 extra guests, so make sure your function never confuses the two.

length.description: The number of items in a list - the same length property you've used on strings (provided by level stdlib)
